people.dateNotes: Birth c. 69 is inferred from his '86 years' remark (which could mean his age or the years since his conversion) and is uncertain. Martyred on 22/23 February in 155 or 156, the standard modern dating; Eusebius's Chronicle points to c. 166-167, which most scholars now reject.

people.name: Irenaeus of Lyon
people.description: Bishop of Lyon who, by his own account, heard Polycarp as a young man. His work Against Heresies is foundational for early Christian orthodoxy and appeals to Scripture, the rule of faith and the succession of bishops from the apostles as tests of true teaching.
people.dateNotes: Born in Asia Minor (probably Smyrna) c. 130-142; died c. 202. Both dates are estimates.

people.name: Tertullian
people.description: Early Latin Christian writer in Carthage. The earliest surviving Latin use of the word trinitas is his, and he shaped much of Latin theological vocabulary. Later he joined the Montanist movement, which is why he is not always counted among the Church Fathers.
people.dateNotes: Born c. 155 in Carthage; died c. 220. Both dates are estimates.

people.name: Origen of Alexandria
people.description: Prolific scholar and head of the catechetical school in Alexandria, later teaching at Caesarea in Palestine. Pioneered textual criticism and allegorical interpretation of Scripture. His Hexapla set the Hebrew Old Testament beside several Greek versions in parallel columns. Some of his speculative teachings were later condemned, but his influence on Eastern and Western exegesis was immense.
people.dateNotes: Born c. 185 in Alexandria; died c. 253-254 in Tyre, after suffering torture in the Decian persecution (250-251).

people.name: Diocletian
people.description: Roman emperor from 284 to 305 who reorganised the empire under a shared rule of four. In 303 he and his colleagues began the last and most severe empire-wide persecution of Christians. He abdicated in 305.
people.dateNotes: Born about 244; abdicated 305; died 311. The first persecution edict was issued at Nicomedia in February 303.

people.name: Constantius I Chlorus
people.description: Roman emperor in the West (Caesar from 293, Augustus 305-306), father of Constantine the Great. His eastern colleagues carried out the Great Persecution, but his own rule in Gaul and Britain was mild. He died at York, where his troops proclaimed Constantine.
people.dateNotes: Born c. 250; died 25 July 306 at Eboracum (York).

people.name: Helena, mother of Constantine
people.description: Mother of Constantine the Great, given the title Augusta by her son. Eusebius reports her pilgrimage to the Holy Land in her old age, and later tradition credits her with finding the True Cross. She is honored as a saint in the Catholic and Orthodox churches. Whether she was Constantius's wife or concubine is debated.
people.dateNotes: Born c. 250 (from Eusebius, who says she was about 80 on her pilgrimage c. 327-328); died c. 330. Eusebius, Life of Constantine 3.42-47. The finding of the Cross is a later tradition.

people.name: Tiridates III of Armenia
people.description: King of Armenia who, according to Armenian tradition, was converted by Gregory the Illuminator and made Armenia the first state to adopt Christianity as its official religion.
people.dateNotes: His reign is usually given as about 287-330; birth year is an estimate. The date of his conversion is traditionally 301 and debated.

people.name: Gregory the Illuminator
people.description: Traditional founder and first head of the Armenian Church. According to Armenian tradition he converted King Tiridates III, who made Christianity the state religion of Armenia.
people.dateNotes: Dates are traditional and approximate; the Armenian sources are later accounts. The conversion is traditionally put at 301, though some scholars date it a decade or so later.

events.role: Baptised the king and led the church

people.name: Galerius
people.description: Roman emperor who is generally thought to have urged Diocletian toward persecuting Christians. In 311, shortly before his death, he issued an edict of toleration ending the persecution in the East.
people.dateNotes: Born about 260; died in 311, soon after the Edict of Serdica (also called the Edict of Toleration).

people.name: Constantine the Great
people.description: Roman emperor who, after the Milvian Bridge (312), favored Christianity, agreed with Licinius to extend toleration (313), and convened the Council of Nicaea (325). He was baptized shortly before his death in 337. Christianity became legal and favored, not the state religion, under him. His mother was Helena and his father Constantius Chlorus.
people.dateNotes: Born c. 272 (Naissus); died 22 May 337 near Nicomedia.

people.name: Athanasius of Alexandria
people.description: Bishop of Alexandria who defended Christ's full deity against Arianism through five exiles, holding the line for the Nicene faith. His Easter festal letter contains the earliest known list of exactly the twenty-seven New Testament books, a landmark in the history of the canon.
people.dateNotes: Born c. 296 (estimates c. 293-298); died 2 May 373. Exiled five times by common count.

people.name: Patricius, father of Augustine
people.description: Pagan town councillor of Thagaste, Augustine's father, who was baptized shortly before his death. He is known from Augustine's Confessions (book 2 and book 9), which describes his ambitions for his son's education.
people.dateNotes: Estimate. Augustine says he died when Augustine was seventeen, c. 371 (Confessions 3.4). His birth year is inferred.

people.name: Gregory of Nazianzus
people.description: Cappadocian bishop and theologian, honoured in the Eastern Church as "the Theologian." He led the Nicene congregation in Constantinople and briefly presided over the Council of 381 before resigning.
people.dateNotes: Born about 329-330; died 390.

events.role: Bishop who led the council at first

people.name: Monica of Hippo
people.description: Christian mother of Augustine of Hippo, who prayed and wept for his conversion for many years and followed him to Milan. She died at Ostia in 387 on the journey home to Africa, shortly after the conversation with her son recorded in the Confessions (book 9). Honored as a saint in the Catholic and Orthodox churches.
people.dateNotes: Born 331 in Thagaste; died 387 at Ostia. Augustine, Confessions 9.8-13.

people.name: Gregory of Nyssa
people.description: Cappadocian bishop and theologian, younger brother of Basil the Great. He took an important part in the Council of Constantinople in 381 and in shaping the doctrine of the Trinity.
people.dateNotes: Birth about 335; death about 395 (last attested that year).

people.name: Jerome
people.description: A learned and irascible monk and biblical scholar who revised the Latin Gospels and Psalms and translated most of the Old Testament into Latin from the Hebrew, settling in Bethlehem around 386. The resulting Vulgate, a composite text that gradually replaced the Old Latin versions, became the Bible of the Western church for about a thousand years.
people.dateNotes: Born c. 347 (some scholars c. 342) in Stridon; died 30 September 420 in Bethlehem.

people.name: John Chrysostom
people.description: Archbishop of Constantinople, famed for his preaching and his expositions of Scripture, who criticized the wealthy and the imperial court and died in exile. Honored in the Eastern and Western churches; his name means Golden-mouthed.
people.dateNotes: Born c. 347 (344-354) in Antioch; died 14 September 407 at Comana in Pontus.

people.name: Theodosius I
people.description: Roman emperor who, in 380, made Nicene Christianity the religion of the empire. He summoned the Council of Constantinople in 381, which confirmed the Nicene faith.
people.dateNotes: Born 11 January 347, emperor in the East 379 and of the whole empire 392-395, died 17 January 395.

people.name: Augustine of Hippo
people.description: A North African rhetorician converted in a Milan garden who became bishop of Hippo and the most influential theologian of the Western church. His Confessions pioneered spiritual autobiography, and his teaching on grace, sin, and the City of God shaped Catholic and Protestant thought alike. His mother Monica and father Patricius are known from the Confessions; his son Adeodatus was born in 372.
people.dateNotes: Born November 13, 354 in Thagaste; died August 28, 430 in Hippo.

people.name: Adeodatus
people.description: Son of Augustine and his unnamed concubine. He was baptized with his father at Milan in 387 and appears as a speaker in Augustine's dialogue De Magistro. He died young, not long after returning to Africa.
people.dateNotes: Born 372 in Carthage; died c. 390. Confessions 4.2, 9.6. Augustine's companion is not named in any source.

people.name: Cyril of Alexandria
people.description: Patriarch of Alexandria from 412 to 444. He opposed Nestorius and presided over the Council of Ephesus in 431, which affirmed the title Theotokos ("God-bearer") for Mary.
people.dateNotes: Born about 376; died 27 June 444.

people.name: Patrick of Ireland
people.description: Missionary to Ireland. Captured as a slave at about 16, he escaped and later returned to evangelize the Irish. Irish Christianity went on to become a notable center of monastic learning and mission.
people.dateNotes: Traditional dates c. 385-461; many modern scholars place his mission in the later fifth century (died c. 490s). Born in Roman Britain; his own Confessio gives no years.

people.name: Nestorius
people.description: Patriarch of Constantinople from 428 who objected to calling Mary Theotokos. The Council of Ephesus deposed him in 431 and he died in exile in Egypt. The Church of the East, often called Nestorian, did not accept his condemnation as fair, and scholars still debate what he actually taught.
people.dateNotes: Born about 386; died after 451, probably that year. Exact dates are not recorded.

people.name: Marcian
people.description: Eastern Roman emperor from 450 to 457. He summoned the Council of Chalcedon in 451, together with his wife Pulcheria, to settle the disputes over the nature of Christ.
people.dateNotes: Born about 392; emperor 450-457; died January 457.

people.name: Pope Leo I
people.description: Bishop of Rome from 440 to 461. His letter to Flavian, known as the Tome of Leo, set out the teaching of two natures in one person of Christ and shaped the definition of Chalcedon in 451. He is also remembered for persuading Attila to withdraw from Italy in 452.
people.dateNotes: Birth year about 400; died 10 November 461.

events.role: Pope whose Tome shaped the definition

people.name: Theodosius II
people.description: Eastern Roman emperor from 408 to 450. He summoned the Council of Ephesus in 431 and the second Council of Ephesus in 449.
people.dateNotes: Born 10 April 401; died 28 July 450 after a riding accident.

people.name: Odoacer
people.description: Germanic military commander who deposed the last Western Roman emperor in 476 and ruled Italy as king. He was killed by Theodoric the Ostrogoth in 493.
people.dateNotes: Birth year is an estimate. He was killed 15 March 493.

people.name: Romulus Augustulus
people.description: The last emperor of the Western Roman Empire. A boy raised to the throne by his father in 475, he was deposed by Odoacer in 476. He was allowed to live, and little more is known of him.
people.dateNotes: Birth year is an estimate (a young teenager in 475-476). Deposed in September 476; the date of his death is unknown.

people.name: Benedict of Nursia
people.description: Founder of Monte Cassino and author of the Rule of St. Benedict, which became the standard rule of Western monasticism. Its balance of prayer, work and study, later summed up in the motto "ora et labora", shaped monastic communities that preserved learning in the early Middle Ages.
people.dateNotes: Born c. 480 in Nursia; died c. 547 (some sources c. 543) at Monte Cassino. Almost all details come from Gregory the Great's Dialogues, book II.

people.name: Gregory the Great
people.description: Pope from 590 to 604, who strengthened the Roman see, sent Augustine of Canterbury to England, and wrote the Pastoral Rule and the Dialogues (the main source for the life of Benedict). He is honored by Catholic and Orthodox churches.
people.dateNotes: Born c. 540 in Rome; died 12 March 604.

people.name: Muhammad
people.description: Arab religious and political leader of Mecca and Medina, regarded by Muslims as the final prophet and the one through whom the Quran was revealed. He founded the Muslim community; within a few years of his death in 632 the armies of his successors, the caliphs, began the conquests of the Byzantine and Persian territories.
people.dateNotes: Traditionally born in Mecca about 570; died at Medina on 8 June 632. Early Muslim sources are the main record and were written some generations later.

events.role: Founder of Islam; the conquests followed his death

people.name: Emperor Taizong of Tang
people.description: Second emperor of the Tang dynasty, who reigned from 626 to 649. According to the Xi'an stele, he welcomed Alopen in 635 and had the Christian teaching examined and permitted.
people.dateNotes: Born 598; emperor 626-649; died 10 July 649.

people.name: Oswiu of Northumbria
people.description: King of Northumbria from 642 to 670. He brought together the Synod of Whitby in 664, which decided that the kingdom would follow the Roman method of calculating Easter.
people.dateNotes: Born about 612; died 15 February 670.

people.name: Hilda of Whitby
people.description: Abbess of Whitby, a noble Northumbrian woman and a counsellor to kings and bishops. Her monastery hosted the synod of 664. Bede praises her wisdom and the learning of those she trained.
people.dateNotes: Born about 614; died 17 November 680.

events.role: Abbess and host of the synod

people.name: Wilfrid
people.description: Northumbrian churchman, later bishop of York, who spoke for the Roman Easter at the Synod of Whitby in 664. His career is told in the Life by Stephen of Ripon.
people.dateNotes: Born about 634; died 709.

people.name: Pope Adrian I
people.description: Bishop of Rome from 772 to 795. He did not attend the Second Council of Nicaea in 787 but was represented there by legates, and he approved its decisions on icons. He was an ally of Charlemagne.
people.dateNotes: Birth year is an estimate; he died 25 December 795.

people.name: Charlemagne
people.description: King of the Franks from 768, who united much of western Europe and supported church reform and learning. He was crowned emperor by Pope Leo III in Rome on Christmas Day, 800.
people.dateNotes: Birth is given as 747 or 748 (sources differ; 742 has also been proposed). He died 28 January 814.

people.name: Pope Leo III
people.description: Bishop of Rome from 795 to 816. After Charlemagne helped him against his enemies in Rome, he crowned Charlemagne emperor on 25 December 800.
people.dateNotes: Birth year about 750; died 12 June 816.

people.name: Empress Irene
people.description: Byzantine empress who ruled as regent for her son from 780 and in her own right from 797 to 802. She summoned the Second Council of Nicaea in 787, which restored the veneration of icons. The Orthodox Church honours her as a saint.
people.dateNotes: Born about 752; died 9 August 803 in exile.

people.name: Methodius
people.description: Brother of Cyril and fellow missionary to the Slavs. After Cyril's death he was made archbishop for Moravia and Pannonia and continued the Slavic translation work despite opposition.
people.dateNotes: Born about 815; died 6 April 885.

people.name: Cyril (Constantine the Philosopher)
people.description: Scholar from Thessalonica who, with his brother Methodius, went to Moravia in 863 and devised the Glagolitic alphabet to translate the scriptures and liturgy into Slavic. He took the name Cyril as a monk shortly before his death in Rome.
people.dateNotes: Born 826 or 827; died 14 February 869.

people.name: Michael I Cerularius
people.description: Patriarch of Constantinople from 1043 to 1058. His dispute with the papal legates in 1054 ended with mutual excommunications and is traditionally counted as the start of the East-West Schism.
people.dateNotes: Born about 1000; died January 1059.

people.name: Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida
people.description: Papal legate to Constantinople in 1054. On 16 July he laid the bull of excommunication against Patriarch Michael Cerularius on the altar of Hagia Sophia.
people.dateNotes: Born about 1000; died 5 May 1061.

events.role: Papal legate who delivered the excommunication

people.name: Pope Leo IX
people.description: Bishop of Rome from 1049 who set the papacy on a course of reform. He sent the legates to Constantinople in 1054, but he had died in April of that year, before the excommunication was delivered in July.
people.dateNotes: Born 21 June 1002; died 19 April 1054.

events.role: Pope who sent the legates; died before they acted

people.name: Pope Urban II
people.description: Pope from 1088 to 1099. At the Council of Clermont in November 1095 he called on Western Christians to aid the Byzantine Empire against the Turks, a call that launched the First Crusade.
people.dateNotes: Born about 1035; died 29 July 1099. No contemporary record preserves his exact words at Clermont.

events.role: Pope who called for the crusade

people.name: Francis of Assisi
people.description: Founder of the Franciscan Order. Renounced wealth to live in radical poverty and preached to the poor. According to tradition he received the stigmata in 1224. Patron saint of animals and ecology.
people.dateNotes: Born 1181 or 1182 in Assisi; died October 3, 1226.

people.name: Thomas Aquinas
people.description: Dominican friar and one of the most influential medieval theologians, honored in the Catholic Church as a Doctor of the Church. His Summa Theologiae brought Aristotelian philosophy into a systematic account of Christian doctrine.
people.dateNotes: Born c. 1224-25 at Roccasecca; died 7 March 1274 at Fossanova Abbey.

people.name: John Wycliffe
people.description: An Oxford theologian who challenged papal wealth and authority and inspired the first complete Bible in English, rendered from the Latin Vulgate by his associates. Condemned after death at the Council of Constance, his remains were exhumed and burned in 1428; his Lollard followers and later admirers gave him the title morning star of the Reformation.
people.dateNotes: Born c. 1328 in Yorkshire; died December 31, 1384.

people.name: Jan Hus
people.description: Czech reformer and rector of the University of Prague. Influenced by Wycliffe, he preached in the common language and challenged papal authority. Burned at the stake at the Council of Constance.
people.dateNotes: Born c. 1372; burned July 6, 1415.

people.name: Johannes Gutenberg
people.description: Goldsmith of Mainz who developed movable-type printing in Europe. His Gutenberg Bible (c. 1455) transformed the spread of Scripture, and the printing press greatly aided the Reformation.
people.dateNotes: Born c. 1400 in Mainz; died February 3, 1468.

people.name: Constantine XI Palaiologos
people.description: Last Byzantine emperor, crowned in 1449. He led the defence of Constantinople and is believed to have died in the final assault of 29 May 1453.
people.dateNotes: Born 8 February 1405; died 29 May 1453. The manner of his death is not fully certain.

people.name: Mehmed II
people.description: Ottoman sultan who captured Constantinople on 29 May 1453 after a siege of about seven weeks, ending the Byzantine Empire. He ruled again from 1451 to 1481.
people.dateNotes: Born 30 March 1432; died 3 May 1481.

events.role: Ottoman sultan who took the city

people.name: Pope Paul III
people.description: Pope from 1534 to 1549. He called the Council of Trent, which opened in December 1545, and approved the Society of Jesus in 1540.
people.dateNotes: Born 29 February 1468; died 10 November 1549.

people.name: Martin Luther
people.description: An Augustinian monk whose Ninety-five Theses against indulgences ignited the Protestant Reformation. At the Diet of Worms he refused to recant unless convinced by Scripture and plain reason, and while hidden at the Wartburg he translated the New Testament into German, reshaping both church and language. He married Katharina von Bora in 1525.
people.dateNotes: Born November 10, 1483; died February 18, 1546.

people.name: Bartolome de las Casas
people.description: Spanish Dominican friar and Bishop of Chiapas who opposed the enslavement and abuse of Indigenous peoples in the Spanish Americas and wrote A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies.
people.dateNotes: Born 1484 (older sources 1474); died 17 July 1566 in Madrid.

people.name: William Tyndale
people.description: A gifted linguist who translated the New Testament into English directly from the Greek, printing it abroad and smuggling copies into England in bales of cloth. Strangled and burned as a heretic, his phrasing lives on, since much of the King James Version, above all its New Testament, descends from his work.
people.dateNotes: Born c. 1494; executed October 6, 1536 near Brussels.

people.name: Katharina von Bora
people.description: Former nun who fled her convent in 1523 and married Martin Luther in 1525. She managed the household and finances of the Black Cloister at Wittenberg and bore six children. Her marriage became the model of the Protestant clergy household.
people.dateNotes: Born 29 January 1499; died 20 December 1552 at Torgau. Married Luther 13 June 1525.

people.name: Francis Xavier
people.description: Spanish Jesuit missionary, a co-founder of the Society of Jesus, who preached in India, Southeast Asia and Japan and died off the coast of China in 1552.
people.dateNotes: Born 7 April 1506; died 3 December 1552 on Shangchuan Island.

people.name: John Calvin
people.description: French theologian and reformer. His Institutes of the Christian Religion (1536) is the foundational text of Reformed theology. Led the church in Geneva.
people.dateNotes: Born July 10, 1509; died May 27, 1564.

people.name: John Knox
people.description: Scottish reformer and a principal leader of the Reformation in Scotland. His preaching and writing helped shape the Church of Scotland, whose Reformed, Presbyterian character emerged from the 1560 Reformation Parliament.
people.dateNotes: Born between c. 1505 and 1514 (c. 1514 is conventional); died 24 November 1572 in Edinburgh.

people.name: Lancelot Andrewes
people.description: Anglican bishop and scholar who led the Westminster company of translators responsible for Genesis through 2 Kings in the King James Version. He was known for his learning in ancient languages and his devotional writing.
people.dateNotes: Born 1555; died 25 September 1626.

events.role: Translator and head of a translation company

people.name: James VI and I
people.description: King of Scotland from 1567 and of England from 1603. At the Hampton Court Conference of 1604 he agreed to a new English translation of the Bible, which appeared in 1611 as the King James or Authorized Version.
people.dateNotes: Born 19 June 1566; died 27 March 1625.

people.name: Samuel Wesley
people.description: Anglican priest and poet, rector of Epworth in Lincolnshire, father of John and Charles Wesley.
people.dateNotes: Born December 1662; died 25 April 1735 at Epworth.

people.name: Susanna Wesley
people.description: Wife of Samuel Wesley and mother of John and Charles Wesley. She educated her children herself at the Epworth rectory by a strict method, and is often called the mother of Methodism.
people.dateNotes: Born 20 January 1669; died 23 July 1742 in London. She bore nineteen children, of whom ten lived to adulthood.

people.name: John Wesley
people.description: Anglican clergyman and leader of the Methodist movement, which separated from the Church of England only after his death. His heart was "strangely warmed" at Aldersgate Street (1738). Traditional estimates say he traveled about 250,000 miles and preached over 40,000 sermons. Son of Samuel and Susanna Wesley; his brother Charles wrote many of the movement's hymns.
people.dateNotes: Born June 28, 1703; died March 2, 1791.

people.name: Jonathan Edwards
people.description: American Congregationalist theologian and preacher of the First Great Awakening. His sermon "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God" (preached at Enfield, 1741) is among the most famous in American history.
people.dateNotes: Born October 5, 1703; died March 22, 1758.

people.name: Charles Wesley
people.description: Younger brother of John Wesley and co-founder of Methodism, author of about six thousand hymns including "Hark! The Herald Angels Sing" and "O for a Thousand Tongues to Sing".
people.dateNotes: Born 18 December 1707; died 29 March 1788 in London.

people.name: George Whitefield
people.description: Anglican evangelist whose open-air preaching in Britain and the American colonies was central to the First Great Awakening and helped spread evangelicalism.
people.dateNotes: Born 16 December 1714; died 30 September 1770 at Newburyport.

people.name: Elias Boudinot
people.description: American lawyer and statesman, president of the Continental Congress in 1782-83 and director of the US Mint. He was the first president of the American Bible Society when it was formed in 1816.
people.dateNotes: Born 2 May 1740; died 24 October 1821.

people.name: Thomas Charles
people.description: Welsh clergyman and Methodist leader at Bala. His effort to supply Welsh-speaking people with Bibles in 1802 is regarded as the immediate cause for founding the British and Foreign Bible Society in 1804.
people.dateNotes: Born 14 October 1755; died 5 October 1814.

events.role: Welsh Methodist whose Bible appeal led to its founding

people.name: William Wilberforce
people.description: English politician and evangelical who led the parliamentary campaign against the slave trade. He was an early and prominent supporter of the British and Foreign Bible Society.
people.dateNotes: Born 24 August 1759; died 29 July 1833.

people.name: William Carey
people.description: English Baptist missionary often called the "father of modern missions." Worked in India for over 40 years; he and his Serampore colleagues translated Scripture, in whole or in part, into dozens of languages of South Asia.
people.dateNotes: Born August 17, 1761; died June 9, 1834.

people.name: Samuel Ajayi Crowther
people.description: Yoruba-born freed slave who became the first African Anglican bishop (consecrated 1864), led the Niger Mission, and translated the Bible into Yoruba and other languages.
people.dateNotes: Born c. 1809 in Osogun; died 31 December 1891 in Lagos.

people.name: Charles Spurgeon
people.description: English Baptist preacher known as the "Prince of Preachers." Pastored the Metropolitan Tabernacle in London (seating 5,000). Sermons still widely read.
people.dateNotes: Born June 19, 1834; died January 31, 1892.

people.name: D.L. Moody
people.description: American evangelist whose revival campaigns reached millions. Founded the Moody Bible Institute (1886) and the Moody Church in Chicago.
people.dateNotes: Born February 5, 1837; died December 22, 1899.

people.name: John R. Mott
people.description: American Methodist layman and leader of the YMCA and the Student Volunteer Movement. He chaired the World Missionary Conference in Edinburgh in 1910, and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1946.
people.dateNotes: Born 25 May 1865; died 31 January 1955.

people.name: William J. Seymour
people.description: African American preacher who led the Azusa Street Mission in Los Angeles from 1906. The multiracial revivals there are widely seen as the beginning of the worldwide Pentecostal movement.
people.dateNotes: Born 2 May 1870; died 28 September 1922.

people.name: Pope John XXIII
people.description: Pope from 1958 to 1963. He called the Second Vatican Council, which opened on 11 October 1962, and died before it ended. The Catholic Church canonised him in 2014.
people.dateNotes: Born 25 November 1881; died 3 June 1963.

people.name: David Ben-Gurion
people.description: Zionist leader who read the Declaration of the Establishment of the State of Israel on 14 May 1948 and became its first prime minister.
people.dateNotes: Born 16 October 1886; died 1 December 1973.

events.role: Declared the state; first prime minister

people.name: Eleazar Sukenik
people.description: Archaeologist of the Hebrew University in Jerusalem. In November 1947 he obtained the first Dead Sea Scrolls for the university and recognised their antiquity.
people.dateNotes: Born 12 August 1889; died 28 February 1953.

events.role: Acquired scrolls for the Hebrew University

people.name: Pope Paul VI
people.description: Pope from 1963 to 1978. He continued the Second Vatican Council after John XXIII's death and closed it in December 1965.
people.dateNotes: Born 26 September 1897; died 6 August 1978.

events.role: Pope who continued and closed the council

people.name: C.S. Lewis
people.description: British scholar and author. Converted from atheism to theism in 1929 and to Christianity in 1931. Works such as Mere Christianity and The Screwtape Letters remain among the most widely read Christian apologetics, and he also wrote the Chronicles of Narnia.
people.dateNotes: Born November 29, 1898; died November 22, 1963.

people.name: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
people.description: German Lutheran pastor and theologian who opposed Nazism and was a leader of the Confessing Church. Arrested in 1943 and hanged at Flossenburg concentration camp on 9 April 1945, weeks before its liberation. Author of The Cost of Discipleship and Life Together.
people.dateNotes: Born February 4, 1906; hanged April 9, 1945.

people.name: John C. Trever
people.description: American biblical scholar at the American Schools of Oriental Research in Jerusalem. In 1948 he photographed the Isaiah scroll and recognised its similarity to ancient scripts, helping to establish its date.
people.dateNotes: Born 1916; died 2006.

events.role: Photographed and helped date the Isaiah scroll

people.name: Billy Graham
people.description: An American evangelist whose stadium crusades and broadcasts carried a simple gospel invitation to more people than perhaps any preacher in history. A counselor to presidents who insisted on integrated seating at his meetings, he became the face of twentieth-century evangelicalism.
people.dateNotes: Born November 7, 1918; died February 21, 2018.

people.name: Melchizedek
people.description: The enigmatic king of Salem and priest of God Most High who blessed Abram and received his tithe. Psalm 110 made his order a royal-priestly ideal, the Dead Sea Scrolls cast him as a heavenly deliverer, and Hebrews sees in him the pattern of Christ's eternal priesthood.
people.dateNotes: Scripture records no birth or death for Melchizedek (Heb 7:3). He is placed on the timeline by his meeting with Abraham (Gen 14:18-20). A Jewish tradition identifies him with Shem; this timeline does not assume it.

people.name: Felix
people.description: Roman governor of Judea who heard Paul's case and left him imprisoned for two years. Husband of Drusilla, a daughter of Herod Agrippa I (Acts 24:24).
people.dateNotes: Acts 23:24-24:27. Procurator of Judea c. AD 52-60 (Josephus; Tacitus), recalled to Rome when Festus succeeded him. His birth and death years are unknown.

people.name: Mattatha
people.description: Son of Nathan, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:31.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy.

people.name: Menna
people.description: Son of Mattatha, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:31.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy.

people.name: Melea
people.description: Son of Menna, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:31.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy.

people.name: Eliakim, son of Melea
people.description: Son of Melea, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:30. Not the Eliakim of Matthew's line or 2 Kings 18.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy. Luke 3:30.

people.name: Jonam
people.description: Son of Eliakim, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:30.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy.

people.name: Joseph, son of Jonam
people.description: Son of Jonam, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:30. Not Joseph of Nazareth.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy. One of several Josephs in the lineage.

people.name: Judah, son of Joseph
people.description: Son of Joseph, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:30. Not the patriarch Judah son of Jacob.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy.

people.name: Simeon, son of Judah
people.description: Son of Judah, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:30. Not Simeon the patriarch or Simeon at the Temple.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy.

people.name: Levi, son of Simeon
people.description: Son of Simeon, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:29. Not the patriarch Levi son of Jacob.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy.

people.name: Matthat, father of Jorim
people.description: Son of Levi, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:29.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy. Pre-exilic Matthat, distinct from the post-exilic Matthat.

people.name: Jorim
people.description: Son of Matthat, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:29.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy.

people.name: Eliezer
people.description: Son of Jorim, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:29. Not Eliezer servant of Abraham.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy.

people.name: Joshua, son of Eliezer
people.description: Son of Eliezer, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:29. Same name as Jesus/Joshua in Hebrew. Not Joshua of the conquest.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy. Greek Iesous = Hebrew Yehoshua.

people.name: Er
people.description: Son of Joshua, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:28. Not Er son of Judah (Gen 38:3).
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy.

people.name: Elmadam
people.description: Son of Er, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:28.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy.

people.name: Cosam
people.description: Son of Elmadam, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:28.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy.

people.name: Addi
people.description: Son of Cosam, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:28.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy.

people.name: Melchi, son of Addi
people.description: Son of Addi, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:28. Pre-exilic Melchi, distinct from the post-exilic Melchi.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy. Luke 3:28.

people.name: Joanan
people.description: Son of Rhesa, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:27.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy.

people.name: Joda
people.description: Son of Joanan, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:26.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy.

people.name: Josech
people.description: Son of Joda, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:26.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy.

people.name: Semein
people.description: Son of Josech, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:26.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy.

people.name: Mattathias, son of Semein
people.description: Son of Semein, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:26.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy. First of two Mattathias in Luke's post-exilic line.

people.name: Maath
people.description: Son of Mattathias, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:26.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy.

people.name: Naggai
people.description: Son of Maath, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:25.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy.

people.name: Esli
people.description: Son of Naggai, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:25.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy.

people.name: Nahum, son of Esli
people.description: Son of Esli, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:25. Not the prophet Nahum.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy. Not to be confused with the prophet Nahum (Nah 1:1).

people.name: Amos, son of Nahum
people.description: Son of Nahum, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:25. Not the prophet Amos.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy. Not to be confused with the prophet Amos (Amos 1:1).

people.name: Mattathias, son of Amos
people.description: Son of Amos, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:25. Second Mattathias in Luke's post-exilic line.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy. Luke 3:25.

people.name: Joseph, son of Mattathias
people.description: Son of Mattathias, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:24. Not Joseph of Nazareth.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy. One of several Josephs in the lineage.

people.name: Jannai
people.description: Son of Joseph, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:24.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy.

people.name: Melchi, son of Jannai
people.description: Son of Jannai, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:24. Post-exilic Melchi, distinct from the pre-exilic Melchi.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy. Luke 3:24.

people.name: Levi, son of Melchi
people.description: Son of Melchi, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:24. Not the patriarch Levi son of Jacob.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy.

people.name: Maacah, wife of Rehoboam
people.description: Wife of King Rehoboam and mother of King Abijah of Judah. Scripture calls her Maachah or Michaiah and gives her father as Absalom (or Abishalom) in 1 Kings 15:2 and 2 Chronicles 11:20, but as Uriel of Gibeah in 2 Chronicles 13:2. Readers commonly explain this by "daughter" meaning granddaughter: Uriel her father, Absalom her grandfather through Tamar. The same name is later given to the "mother" of King Asa, whom Asa removed from being queen for making an idol; many take this to be Asa's grandmother.
people.dateNotes: Birth and death are not recorded. Rehoboam's wife and Abijah's mother (2 Chr 11:20). Because her father is given differently in the sources, her father is not recorded in the table, and Asa's mother_id is left empty for the same reason.

scripture.context: Called Michaiah, daughter of Uriel of Gibeah
Asa removed Maachah, called his "mother," from being queen for making an idol (often read as this Maacah, his grandmother)

people.name: Azubah, mother of Jehoshaphat
people.description: Daughter of Shilhi and mother of King Jehoshaphat of Judah.
people.dateNotes: Birth and death are not recorded. Wife of Asa (Jehoshaphat's father) and mother of Jehoshaphat, who was 35 when he began to reign (1 Kgs 22:42).

scripture.context: Named as Jehoshaphat's mother, daughter of Shilhi

people.name: Zibiah of Beer-sheba
people.description: Queen mother of Judah, mother of King Joash (Jehoash) of Judah. She came from Beer-sheba.
people.dateNotes: Birth and death are not recorded. Mother of Joash, who began to reign in the seventh year of Jehu (2 Kgs 12:1); her husband was Ahaziah of Judah.

people.name: Jehoaddan of Jerusalem
people.description: Queen mother of Judah, mother of King Amaziah. She came from Jerusalem.
people.dateNotes: Birth and death are not recorded. Mother of Amaziah, who began to reign at 25 (2 Kgs 14:2); her husband was Joash of Judah.

people.name: Jecholiah of Jerusalem
people.description: Queen mother of Judah, mother of King Uzziah (Azariah). She came from Jerusalem.
people.dateNotes: Birth and death are not recorded. Mother of Uzziah, who began to reign at 16 (2 Kgs 15:2); her husband was Amaziah.

people.name: Jerusha, daughter of Zadok
people.description: Queen mother of Judah, mother of King Jotham. Her father is named Zadok; he is not identified with the priest Zadok of David's time.
people.dateNotes: Birth and death are not recorded. Mother of Jotham, who began to reign at 25 (2 Kgs 15:33); her husband was Uzziah.

scripture.context: Named as Jotham's mother, daughter of Zadok

people.name: Abi, mother of Hezekiah
people.description: Queen mother of Judah, daughter of Zachariah and mother of King Hezekiah. Second Chronicles gives her name as Abijah.
people.dateNotes: Birth and death are not recorded. Wife of Ahaz and mother of Hezekiah (2 Kgs 18:2). Hezekiah's birth year in the table makes Ahaz only 11 years older, a known difficulty in the figures of 2 Kings 16:2 and 18:2.

scripture.context: Named as Hezekiah's mother, daughter of Zachariah

people.name: Hephzibah, mother of Manasseh
people.description: Queen mother of Judah and mother of King Manasseh, who began to reign at 12. Her name means "my delight is in her."
people.dateNotes: Birth and death are not recorded. Wife of Hezekiah and mother of Manasseh (2 Kgs 21:1).

people.name: Meshullemeth, daughter of Haruz
people.description: Queen mother of Judah, daughter of Haruz of Jotbah and mother of King Amon.
people.dateNotes: Birth and death are not recorded. Wife of Manasseh and mother of Amon, who began to reign at 22 (2 Kgs 21:19).

scripture.context: Named as Amon's mother, daughter of Haruz of Jotbah

people.name: Jedidah, daughter of Adaiah
people.description: Queen mother of Judah, daughter of Adaiah of Boscath and mother of King Josiah.
people.dateNotes: Birth and death are not recorded. Wife of Amon and mother of Josiah, who began to reign at eight (2 Kgs 22:1).

scripture.context: Named as Josiah's mother, daughter of Adaiah of Boscath

people.name: Hamutal, daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah
people.description: Queen mother of Judah, mother of two kings, Jehoahaz and Zedekiah, both sons of Josiah. Her father Jeremiah of Libnah is not the prophet Jeremiah of Anathoth.
people.dateNotes: Birth and death are not recorded. Wife of Josiah; mother of Jehoahaz (2 Kgs 23:31) and of Zedekiah (2 Kgs 24:18).

people.name: Zebudah, daughter of Pedaiah
people.description: Queen mother of Judah, daughter of Pedaiah of Rumah and mother of King Jehoiakim.
people.dateNotes: Birth and death are not recorded. Wife of Josiah and mother of Jehoiakim, who began to reign at 25 (2 Kgs 23:36).

scripture.context: Named as Jehoiakim's mother, daughter of Pedaiah of Rumah

people.name: Nehushta, daughter of Elnathan
people.description: Queen mother of Judah, daughter of Elnathan of Jerusalem and mother of King Jehoiachin. She went into exile in Babylon with her son.
people.dateNotes: Birth and death are not recorded. Wife of Jehoiakim and mother of Jehoiachin, who began to reign at 18 (2 Kgs 24:8; the exile of the queen mother is in 2 Kgs 24:12-15).

scripture.context: Named as Jehoiachin's mother, daughter of Elnathan
Taken captive to Babylon with her son

people.name: Shaphat, father of Elisha
people.description: Father of the prophet Elisha, who came from Abel-meholah. Elijah was told to anoint Elisha "the son of Shaphat".
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. The father is named in the text; no dates are recorded for him.

scripture.context: Named as Elisha's father, of Abel-meholah

people.name: Amoz, father of Isaiah
people.description: Father of the prophet Isaiah. He is named in the opening of Isaiah and in the Kings account of Hezekiah. He is a different name in Hebrew from the prophet Amos.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. The father is named in the text; no dates are recorded for him.

people.name: Wife of Isaiah (the prophetess)
people.description: Called "the prophetess" in Isaiah 8:3, she bore Isaiah the son named Maher-shalal-hash-baz. Her own name is not given.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. The text does not give her name or dates.

people.name: Hilkiah, father of Jeremiah
people.description: A priest of Anathoth in the land of Benjamin and father of the prophet Jeremiah. The text does not say he is the same man as Hilkiah the high priest who found the Book of the Law under Josiah, so the two are kept separate here.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. The father is named in the text; no dates are recorded for him.

scripture.context: Named as Jeremiah's father, one of the priests of Anathoth

people.name: Buzi
people.description: Father of the prophet Ezekiel. Ezekiel is called a priest, so Buzi was presumably of a priestly family, though the text does not say so of Buzi himself.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. The father is named in the text; no dates are recorded for him.

people.name: Amittai
people.description: Father of the prophet Jonah, who came from Gath-hepher.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. The father is named in the text; no dates are recorded for him.

scripture.context: Jonah the son of Amittai, of Gath-hepher

people.name: Beeri, father of Hosea
people.description: Father of the prophet Hosea.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. The father is named in the text; no dates are recorded for him.

people.name: Gomer, wife of Hosea
people.description: Daughter of Diblaim, whom Hosea married at the Lord's command as a living picture of Israel's unfaithfulness. She bore Jezreel and, according to the following verses, Lo-ruhamah and Lo-ammi.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. She was the wife of Hosea (about 805-720 BC), so was alive in the time of Jeroboam II.

scripture.context: Daughter of Diblaim; Hosea marries her and she bears a son

people.name: Diblaim
people.description: Father of Gomer, the wife of the prophet Hosea.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. The father is named in the text; no dates are recorded for him.

people.name: Pethuel
people.description: Father of the prophet Joel.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. The father is named in the text; no dates are recorded for him.

people.name: Hizkiah, ancestor of Zephaniah
people.description: Great-great-grandfather of the prophet Zephaniah, who traces his line in Zephaniah 1:1 four generations back to Hizkiah. Naming so many generations is unusual and has led many to think Hizkiah is King Hezekiah, but the text does not call him king, so this table keeps him as a separate person. Whether the two are the same is uncertain.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. Not linked to King Hezekiah: the identification is likely to some readers but the text does not make it, and Zephaniah's four-generation line would fit either way.

scripture.context: Named at the head of Zephaniah's line

people.name: Amariah, grandfather of Zephaniahs father
people.description: Son of Hizkiah, father of Gedaliah, and an ancestor of the prophet Zephaniah.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. The father is named in the text; no dates are recorded for him.

scripture.context: In Zephaniah's line, son of Hizkiah

people.name: Gedaliah, grandfather of Zephaniah
people.description: Son of Amariah, father of Cushi, and grandfather of the prophet Zephaniah. He is not the Gedaliah who was made governor of Judah after the fall of Jerusalem.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. The father is named in the text; no dates are recorded for him.

scripture.context: In Zephaniah's line, father of Cushi

people.name: Cushi, father of Zephaniah
people.description: Son of Gedaliah and father of the prophet Zephaniah.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. The father is named in the text; no dates are recorded for him.

people.name: Iddo, grandfather of Zechariah
people.description: Called "Iddo the prophet" in Zechariah 1:1, grandfather of the prophet Zechariah. Ezra 5:1 and 6:14 call Zechariah "the son of Iddo," as the line is shortened. A priestly family of Iddo came back with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:4, 16), and Zechariah is named as its head, but the text does not state that this Iddo is the same.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. The father is named in the text; no dates are recorded for him.

scripture.context: Named as the prophet Zechariah's grandfather

people.name: Berechiah, father of Zechariah
people.description: Son of Iddo and father of the prophet Zechariah. Ezra 5:1 names only Iddo as Zechariah's father, which is usually explained as the line being shortened.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. The father is named in the text; no dates are recorded for him.

scripture.context: Named as Zechariah's father, son of Iddo

people.name: Seraiah, ancestor of Ezra
people.description: First name in the line of Ezra the scribe in Ezra 7:1, which runs back through Azariah, Hilkiah, Shallum and Zadok to Phinehas and Aaron the chief priest. The list is abridged (compare 1 Chronicles 6:3-15), and "son of" in it means descendant. Most readers identify this Seraiah with Seraiah the chief priest killed at Riblah in 588 BC (2 Kings 25:18; 1 Chronicles 6:14), who is Ezra's ancestor, not his father. Ezra's own father is not named, so no parent link is recorded for Ezra.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. If he is the Seraiah of 2 Kgs 25:18 he was killed in 588 BC, about 90 years before Ezra's birth in this table, so "son of" in Ezra 7:1 means descendant. The rest of the line is not added as separate rows.

scripture.context: First name in Ezra's line back to Aaron (Ezra 7:1)

people.name: Hacaliah
people.description: Father of Nehemiah the governor, named in the opening of the book of Nehemiah.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. The father is named in the text; no dates are recorded for him.

people.name: Hanani, brother of Nehemiah
people.description: Nehemiah's brother who came to Susa with men from Judah and told him of the broken walls of Jerusalem. Nehemiah later put him in charge of Jerusalem with Hananiah the ruler of the palace. "Brother" may mean close kinsman.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. He was a contemporary of Nehemiah (about 470-400 BC) and was alive at the time of the walls in 445 BC.

events.role: Brought the report that led Nehemiah to go; later put in charge of Jerusalem

scripture.context: Brings news of Jerusalem to Nehemiah

people.name: Abihail
people.description: Father of Esther and uncle of Mordecai, who brought Esther up as his own daughter after both her parents died.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. The father is named in the text; no dates are recorded for him.

scripture.context: Named as Esther's father and Mordecai's uncle

people.name: Jair, father of Mordecai
people.description: Son of Shimei and father of Mordecai, a Benjamite of Susa. This is not the judge Jair.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. Esther 2:5-6 is unclear whether it is Mordecai or his ancestor Kish who was carried away with Jeconiah in 599 BC, and the line may be abridged.

scripture.context: Named as Mordecai's father, son of Shimei

people.name: Shimei, grandfather of Mordecai
people.description: Son of Kish and grandfather of Mordecai. He is not identified with Shimei son of Gera, who cursed David; the text does not link them.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. The father is named in the text; no dates are recorded for him.

scripture.context: In Mordecai's line, son of Kish

people.name: Kish, ancestor of Mordecai
people.description: A Benjamite named at the head of Mordecai's line in Esther 2:5. He is not identified with Kish, the father of King Saul, though both were Benjamites.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. The text may be telescoping the line.

scripture.context: Named at the head of Mordecai's line

people.name: Hammedatha the Agagite
people.description: Father of Haman the Agagite, who rose high under King Ahasuerus and plotted to destroy the Jews.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. The father is named in the text; no dates are recorded for him.

people.name: Zeresh
people.description: Wife of Haman, who with his friends advised him to build the high gallows for Mordecai and later told him he would fall before the Jews.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. She was Haman's wife, so lived about 510-473 BC.

scripture.context: Haman's wife, called with his friends

people.name: Ahijah, father of Baasha
people.description: Father of Baasha, the king of Israel who killed Nadab, of the house of Issachar. He is not the prophet Ahijah of Shiloh.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. The father is named in the text; no dates are recorded for him.

people.name: Jehoshaphat, father of Jehu
people.description: Son of Nimshi and father of Jehu, king of Israel. He is not King Jehoshaphat of Judah. In 1 Kings 19:16 Jehu is called "son of Nimshi," meaning grandson.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. The father is named in the text; no dates are recorded for him.

scripture.context: Named as Jehu's father, son of Nimshi

people.name: Nimshi
people.description: Father of Jehoshaphat and grandfather of Jehu, who is called "the son of Nimshi" in 1 Kings 19:16 and 2 Kings 9:20.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. The father is named in the text; no dates are recorded for him.

scripture.context: Jehu called the son of Nimshi

people.name: Jabesh, father of Shallum
people.description: Father of Shallum, who killed Zechariah and reigned one month as king of Israel.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. The father is named in the text; no dates are recorded for him.

people.name: Gadi, father of Menahem
people.description: Father of Menahem, who killed Shallum and became king of Israel.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. The father is named in the text; no dates are recorded for him.

people.name: Remaliah
people.description: Father of Pekah, the army captain who killed Pekahiah and became king of Israel. Isaiah 7:4-9 uses "Remaliah's son" to mean Pekah.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. The father is named in the text; no dates are recorded for him.

people.name: Elah, father of Hoshea
people.description: Father of Hoshea, the last king of Israel. He is not Elah the son of Baasha, who had been king earlier.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. The father is named in the text; no dates are recorded for him.

people.name: Jehoiada the priest
people.description: High priest in Jerusalem who, with his wife Jehosheba, hid the infant Joash from Athaliah, then crowned him king at age seven and guided him while Jehoiada lived. He died at 130 and was buried among the kings.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded as a year. He lived 130 years (2 Chr 24:15) and anointed Joash in about 878 BC, when Joash was seven.

scripture.context: Husband of Jehosheba, who hid Joash

people.name: Jehosheba
people.description: Daughter of King Jehoram of Judah, sister of Ahaziah and wife of Jehoiada the priest. When Athaliah killed the royal family she hid the infant Joash in the temple for six years. Second Chronicles calls her Jehoshabeath.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. Her mother is not named in the text and is not recorded here.

scripture.context: Daughter of King Joram; hides Joash

people.name: Ethbaal
people.description: King of the Zidonians, whose daughter Jezebel married Ahab of Israel and brought the worship of Baal into the northern kingdom. Outside sources know him as Ithobaal I of Tyre and Sidon.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. His reign is placed around 887-856 BC by Tyrian king lists, which do not line up exactly with the dates here for Jezebel and Ahab, so no year is given.

scripture.context: Father of Jezebel, king of the Zidonians

people.name: Ben-hadad, son of Hazael
people.description: King of Syria who succeeded his father Hazael and continued to oppress Israel under Jehoahaz, until Joash of Israel won three victories over him. Outside sources call him Ben-hadad III.
people.dateNotes: Not recorded. He succeeded Hazael (2 Kgs 13:24).

scripture.context: Son of Hazael; Israel delivered into his hand

people.name: Nabopolassar
people.description: Founder of the Neo-Babylonian dynasty, who threw off Assyrian rule and, with the Medes, destroyed Nineveh. Father of Nebuchadnezzar II. He is not named in Scripture.
people.dateNotes: Standard historical record (not stated in Scripture). He reigned 626-605 BC and died in August 605 BC. Birth unknown.

people.name: Evil-merodach
people.description: Son of Nebuchadnezzar and king of Babylon, who in the first year of his reign released King Jehoiachin from prison and gave him a seat above the other kings. He is the Amel-Marduk of Babylonian records.
people.dateNotes: Standard historical record (not stated in Scripture). Reigned 562-560 BC, killed in a coup in 560 BC. The 37th year of Jehoiachin's captivity is 2 Kgs 25:27.

scripture.context: Lifts up the head of Jehoiachin

people.name: Nabonidus
people.description: Last king of Babylon, who spent years at Tema in Arabia and left his son Belshazzar in charge in Babylon. He is not named in Daniel, but Belshazzar's offer of "the third ruler in the kingdom" (Dan 5:16, 29) is commonly explained by Nabonidus holding the first place and Belshazzar the second.
people.dateNotes: Standard historical record (not stated in Scripture). Reigned 556-539 BC. His fate after Cyrus took Babylon is told differently in the sources, so no death year is given. Not named in Scripture.

events.role: King of Babylon when the city fell to Cyrus, not in Scripture by name

scripture.context: Not named; Daniel made third ruler of the kingdom

people.name: Sargon II
people.description: King of Assyria who completed the conquest of Samaria and sent his commander against Ashdod. Father of Sennacherib.
people.dateNotes: Standard historical record (not stated in Scripture). Reigned 722-705 BC and was killed in battle in 705 BC. Birth unknown. Named once, in Isaiah 20:1.

people.name: Esarhaddon
people.description: King of Assyria, son and successor of Sennacherib after Sennacherib's sons killed him. The settlers brought into Samaria in the northern kingdom are said to have been brought by him.
people.dateNotes: Standard historical record (not stated in Scripture). Reigned 681-669 BC and died in 669 BC on campaign. Birth unknown.

scripture.context: Reigns in his father Sennacherib's place
The settlers say they were brought up in his days

people.name: Cambyses I
people.description: King of Anshan in Persia and father of Cyrus the Great. He is not named in Scripture.
people.dateNotes: Standard historical record (not stated in Scripture). Reigned about 600-559 BC. Dates are uncertain; death year is approximate. Not named in Scripture.

people.name: Cambyses II
people.description: Son and successor of Cyrus the Great, who conquered Egypt in 525 BC. He is not named in Scripture; the Persian reign between Cyrus and Darius is passed over in Ezra 4:5.
people.dateNotes: Standard historical record (not stated in Scripture). Reigned 530-522 BC and died in 522 BC. Birth unknown.

people.name: Hystaspes
people.description: Persian noble, called Vishtaspa in Persian, and father of Darius I. He served as a governor and was not king himself. Not named in Scripture.
people.dateNotes: Standard historical record (not stated in Scripture). Dates unknown.

people.name: Atossa
people.description: Persian queen, daughter of Cyrus the Great, who married Darius I and bore Xerxes. Not named in Scripture.
people.dateNotes: Standard historical record (not stated in Scripture). Dates unknown. Mother of Xerxes according to Herodotus.

people.name: Mattathias
people.description: Priest of Modein who started the Maccabean revolt by refusing to sacrifice to the king's idols. Father of five sons, including Judas Maccabeus, Jonathan and Simon.
people.dateNotes: Not in the KJV Bible; known from 1 Maccabees (accepted by Catholic and Orthodox traditions) and Josephus. He died in 166 BC soon after beginning the revolt. Birth unknown.

people.name: Simon Maccabeus
people.description: Second son of Mattathias, who succeeded Jonathan as leader and high priest and made Judea independent. He was murdered at a banquet in 135 BC.
people.dateNotes: Not in the KJV Bible; known from 1 Maccabees (accepted by Catholic and Orthodox traditions) and Josephus. Died 135 BC. Birth unknown.

events.role: Brother and later leader of the revolt

people.name: Jonathan Maccabeus
people.description: Youngest son of Mattathias, who led after Judas died, became high priest in 152 BC and was killed by treachery in 143 BC.
people.dateNotes: Not in the KJV Bible; known from 1 Maccabees (accepted by Catholic and Orthodox traditions) and Josephus. Died 143 BC. Birth unknown.

events.role: Brother and later leader of the revolt

people.name: John Hyrcanus
people.description: Son of Simon Maccabeus, high priest and ruler of Judea from 134 to 104 BC, who expanded the Hasmonean state.
people.dateNotes: Not in the KJV Bible; known from 1 Maccabees (accepted by Catholic and Orthodox traditions) and Josephus. Reigned 134-104 BC. Birth unknown.

people.name: Alopen
people.description: Syriac Christian missionary of the Church of the East who reached the Tang capital Chang'an in 635. The Xi'an stele of 781 records that he was received by the emperor and allowed to translate and teach the scriptures.
people.dateNotes: Birth and death dates are unknown. 635 is the arrival date given on the Xi'an stele.

people.name: Colman of Lindisfarne
people.description: Irish-trained bishop of Lindisfarne who defended the Ionan (Irish) Easter reckoning at Whitby. When the synod ruled against it he left Northumbria with his followers.
people.dateNotes: Birth year unknown. He became bishop in 661 and died in 676.

people.name: Rastislav of Moravia
people.description: Prince of Great Moravia, who around 862 asked the Byzantine emperor for teachers able to instruct his people in their own language. Cyril and Methodius were sent in response.
people.dateNotes: Birth unknown. He reigned from about 846 and was deposed and blinded about 870.

people.name: Muhammed edh-Dhib
people.description: Young Bedouin shepherd of the Ta'amireh tribe who found the first scrolls in a cave near Qumran. The find is dated to 1946 or 1947.
people.dateNotes: Birth and death dates are not known. The date of discovery is given variously as late 1946 or early 1947.

events.role: Shepherd who found the first scrolls

events.name: Creation
events.description: In the Bible's opening scene, God speaks an ordered cosmos into being, crowning it with humanity made in the divine image and a day of rest. Unlike Babylon's Enuma Elish, where creation follows divine combat, Genesis presents one sovereign God whose word alone brings light, life, and order.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: 4004 BC (AM 1). October 23, 4004 BC per Annales. Mainstream scholarship does not derive the age of the world from the Genesis genealogies, which may omit generations; Ussher's figure is one traditional reading.

events.name: The Fall
events.description: In Eden, Adam and Eve eat from the forbidden tree at the serpent's urging, breaking trust with their Creator. Their exile from the garden brings sin, death, and alienation into the human story, setting the stage for the long biblical drama of redemption that Scripture traces to Christ.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: 4004 BC.

events.name: Cain Kills Abel
events.description: Cain, angered that God accepted Abel's offering and not his own, kills his brother in the field. It is the first death recorded in Scripture, and God sends Cain away as a restless wanderer, yet under a protective mark.
events.dateNotes: Estimate. Scripture gives no date; Abel was killed before Seth was born when Adam was 130 (Gen 4:25; 5:3). The year matches the estimate in Abel's row.

events.name: Enoch Taken by God
events.description: Enoch walks with God for 300 years after the birth of Methuselah and then is not, for God takes him in the 365th year of his life. Hebrews says he was taken up without seeing death.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: AM 987 from Gen 5:21-24 (born 3382 BC, aged 365). Matches the year given in Enoch's row.

events.name: The Flood
events.description: Grieved by human violence, God cleanses the earth with a flood while preserving Noah, his family, and the animals in the ark, then seals a covenant with the rainbow sign. Mesopotamian epics like Gilgamesh and Atrahasis preserve parallel flood tales, yet Genesis uniquely grounds the deluge in divine justice.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: began 2349 BC (AM 1656), ended 2348 BC. Gen 8:13-14 puts the drying of the earth in Noah's 601st year. Mainstream scholarship does not date the Flood from the Genesis genealogies.

people.role: Son of Noah; entered the ark (Gen 7:13)
Son of Noah; entered the ark (Gen 7:13)
Son of Noah; entered the ark (Gen 7:13)

events.name: Tower of Babel
events.description: United humanity builds a tower on the plain of Shinar to make a name for itself, and God scatters the builders by confusing their language. The story evokes Mesopotamian ziggurats such as Babylon's Etemenanki and explains the dispersion of nations, which Genesis places generations before God's call of Abraham.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: 2247 BC (AM 1757), when Peleg was born and the earth was divided (Gen 10:25), about 326 years before Abraham left Haran in 1921 BC.

events.name: Call of Abraham
events.description: God summons Abram to leave his homeland and his father's house, going by way of Haran, for a country God would show him, promising to make him a great nation and a blessing to all peoples of the earth. His obedient departure launches the covenant story that the rest of Scripture traces through Israel to the Messiah.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: 1921 BC (AM 2083), when Abraham left Haran aged 75 (Gen 12:4) after Terah's death at 205 (Acts 7:4). Acts 7:2-4 and Gen 15:7 indicate that God first called him in Ur, earlier.

events.name: Abrahamic Covenant
events.description: In a solemn night ceremony, God passes between divided animal carcasses as a smoking firepot and blazing torch, swearing to give Abram countless descendants and the land of Canaan. The rite mirrors ancient Near Eastern treaty customs, yet here God alone walks the path, bearing the covenant obligation himself.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: c. 1913 BC (AM 2091).

events.name: Birth of Ishmael
events.description: After ten years in Canaan Sarai gives her servant Hagar to Abram, and Hagar bears Ishmael when Abram is 86. God hears the boy's cry and promises to make him a great nation, though the covenant line runs through Isaac.
events.dateNotes: Gen 16:3, 16: Abram aged 86 (Ussher 1910 BC).

events.name: Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah
events.description: Fire and sulfur destroy Sodom and Gomorrah after the outcry against their wickedness reaches heaven, though angels lead Lot's family out; his wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt. The doomed cities of the Dead Sea plain become Scripture's enduring emblem of judgment, invoked by prophets and by Jesus.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: c. 1897 BC (Gen 19). Abraham was 99 years old.

people.role: Rescued from the city by the angels (Gen 19)

events.name: Covenant of Circumcision
events.description: God gives Abraham circumcision as the enduring sign of the covenant, marking every male of his household and renaming Abram and Sarai as heirs of the promise of nations and kings. Though circumcision was practiced in Egypt and elsewhere, Israel uniquely made it a covenant emblem binding each generation to God.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: c. 1897 BC. Abraham aged 99 (Gen 17:1, 24).

people.role: Received the covenant sign and circumcised his household (Gen 17)
Promised a son within the covenant (Gen 17:15-16)

events.name: Birth of Isaac
events.description: Isaac is born to Abraham at 100 and Sarah at 90, the child of promise whose name means laughter. He is circumcised on the eighth day, and the covenant line runs through him.
events.dateNotes: Gen 21:5; 17:17: Abraham aged 100 (Ussher 1896 BC).

events.name: Binding of Isaac
events.description: God tests Abraham by commanding the sacrifice of Isaac, the son of promise, on Mount Moriah; at the final moment an angel stays the knife and a ram is offered instead. Known in Jewish tradition as the Akedah, the event affirms that God himself provides the sacrifice, a theme Christians hear echoed at Calvary.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: c. 1872 BC. Scripture gives no age for Isaac (Gen 22:5 calls him a lad); about 24 follows from Ussher's date, and Josephus (Antiquities 1) says 25.

events.name: Death of Sarah and Purchase of Machpelah
events.description: Sarah dies at 127 in Hebron, and Abraham buys the cave of Machpelah from Ephron the Hittite for 400 shekels of silver. It is his only possession in the promised land, and later holds Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Leah and Jacob.
events.dateNotes: Gen 23:1-20: Sarah aged 127 (born 1986 BC).

events.name: Isaac Marries Rebekah
events.description: Abraham's servant travels to Mesopotamia and brings back Rebekah, who marries Isaac when he is 40, three years after Sarah's death. Isaac is comforted after his mother's death.
events.dateNotes: Gen 24; 25:20: Isaac aged 40 (born 1896 BC).

events.name: Jacob Flees to Haran
events.description: Having gained Isaac's blessing and the birthright, Jacob flees Esau's anger toward Haran, and at Bethel dreams of a ladder to heaven where God confirms the Abrahamic promise to him.
events.dateNotes: Gen 27-28. Derived: Jacob was 91 at Joseph's birth (Gen 41:46; 45:6; 47:9) at the end of 14 years of service (Gen 30:25; 31:41), so he left about age 77 (1759 BC).

events.name: Jacob Marries Leah and Rachel
events.description: Jacob serves Laban seven years for Rachel but is given Leah; he receives Rachel a week later and serves seven more. Eleven of the twelve tribal ancestors and Dinah are born over the following years.
events.dateNotes: Gen 29:18-30; derived date: 7 years after his arrival in 1759 BC, Jacob about 84.

events.name: Jacob Wrestles God
events.description: Jacob wrestles with God and is renamed Israel.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: c. 1739 BC (Gen 32:22-32).

events.name: Joseph Sold into Slavery
events.description: Joseph's brothers sell him to traders going to Egypt.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: c. 1728 BC (Joseph aged 17, Gen 37:2).

events.name: Joseph Made Ruler of Egypt
events.description: Sold by his brothers yet raised from prison to Pharaoh's right hand, Joseph interprets dreams of coming famine and administers Egypt's grain stores. His rise turns betrayal into rescue, positioning him to preserve Jacob's family, the fledgling covenant line, through seven years of scarcity.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: c. 1715 BC. Joseph aged 30 (Gen 41:46).

people.role: Given to Joseph as wife by Pharaoh (Gen 41:45)

events.name: Seven Years of Famine Begin
events.description: After seven years of plenty, famine spreads across Egypt and the nearby lands, and Joseph opens the storehouses. In the second year of famine Joseph's brothers come to buy grain, and he reveals himself to them.
events.dateNotes: Gen 41:46, 53-57; 45:6: Joseph ruler at 30 (1715 BC) + 7 years of plenty gives famine year 1 = 1708 BC, year 2 = 1707 BC; Jacob enters Egypt 1706 BC.

events.name: Israel Enters Egypt
events.description: Jacob and his whole household migrate to Egypt at Joseph's invitation, settling in the fertile land of Goshen and growing there into a numerous people. Egyptian art such as the Beni Hasan tomb painting depicts Semitic families entering Egypt, illustrating this well-traveled path in times of famine.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: 1706 BC (AM 2298). Jacob aged 130 (Gen 47:9).

people.role: Son of Jacob who came into Egypt (Gen 46:23)
Son of Jacob who came into Egypt (Gen 46:24)
Son of Jacob who came into Egypt (Gen 46:16)
Son of Jacob who came into Egypt (Gen 46:17)
Son of Jacob who came into Egypt (Gen 46:13)
Son of Jacob who came into Egypt (Gen 46:14)
Grandson of Jacob who came into Egypt (Gen 46:11)
Joseph's son, born in Egypt and counted among Jacob's house (Gen 46:20,27)
Joseph's son, born in Egypt and counted among Jacob's house (Gen 46:20,27)
Grandson of Jacob who came into Egypt (Gen 46:12)

events.name: The Exodus
events.description: After ten plagues break Pharaoh's resistance, Israel departs Egypt under Moses on Passover night, freed from slavery to become a covenant nation. The Merneptah Stele, an Egyptian victory monument, preserves the earliest known extrabiblical mention of Israel as a people.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: 1491 BC (AM 2513), 430 years after the call of Abraham (Gal 3:17; Exod 12:40-41). Many scholars favour an early date c. 1446 BC (1 Kgs 6:1); others a late date c. 1260-1250 BC.

events.name: Crossing the Red Sea
events.description: Trapped between Pharaoh's chariots and the sea, Israel watches God part the waters at Moses' outstretched hand, crossing on dry ground while the pursuing army is drowned. The Song of the Sea celebrating this rescue is reckoned among the oldest poetry preserved in the Hebrew Bible.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: 1491 BC.

people.role: Led the women in song after the crossing (Ex 15:20-21)

events.name: Giving of the Law
events.description: Amid thunder and fire on Mount Sinai, God speaks the Ten Commandments and gives Moses the Torah, constituting rescued slaves as a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. Scholars note that the covenant's structure parallels ancient suzerainty treaties, casting God as Israel's sovereign King.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: 1491 BC (AM 2513), third month after Exodus.

events.name: Wilderness Wandering
events.description: After refusing to enter Canaan at the spies' fearful report, Israel wanders the wilderness for forty years until the unbelieving generation passes away. Sustained by manna, water from the rock, and the guiding cloud, the nation is disciplined and shaped for covenant life in the promised land.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: 1491-1451 BC.

people.role: Moses' father-in-law; visited him at the mount of God (Ex 18)
Spoke against Moses and died at Kadesh (Num 12; 20:1)
Moses' wife; came to him with Jethro (Ex 18:2)
Led a rebellion against Moses and Aaron (Num 16)
Moses' son; came to him with Jethro (Ex 18:3)
Moses' son; came to him with Jethro (Ex 18:4)
King of Moab who hired Balaam (Num 22-24)
Priest who ended the plague at Baal-peor (Num 25)

events.name: Tabernacle Completed
events.description: Following the pattern revealed on Sinai, Israel completes the tabernacle, a portable tent sanctuary where God's glory descends to dwell at the center of the camp. Its gilded frames recall Egyptian portable shrines of the era, while its design anticipates the temple and, for Christians, the incarnation.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: 1490 BC (Exod 40:17). One year after the Exodus.

people.role: Consecrated as priest for the tabernacle (Ex 40:12-15)
Oversaw the work and set up the tabernacle (Ex 39-40)
First prince to bring an offering at its dedication (Num 7:12)
Craftsman called to build the tabernacle (Ex 31:2-5)

events.name: Conquest of Canaan
events.description: Under Joshua, Israel crosses the Jordan and campaigns through Canaan, defeating coalitions of kings and allotting the land among the twelve tribes. Destruction layers at sites like Hazor, the greatest Canaanite city of the region, fuel lively scholarly debate over the conquest's scope and character.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: the war began in 1451 BC (AM 2553), after forty years in the wilderness, and ended in 1445 BC, when Caleb was 85 (Josh 14:7-10) and "the land rested from war" (Josh 11:23; 14:15). Early-date scholars place the conquest c. 1406 BC; late-date scholars c. 1220 BC.

events.name: Fall of Jericho
events.description: Israel circles Jericho for seven days behind the ark until the walls collapse at the trumpet blast and shout, giving Joshua his first victory in Canaan; only faithful Rahab's family is spared. Famous excavations by John Garstang and Kathleen Kenyon made Jericho a landmark case in biblical archaeology.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: 1451 BC.

events.name: Death of Moses
events.description: At 120 years old, his eye not dim nor his strength abated, Moses climbs Mount Nebo, views the promised land, and dies in Moab; the LORD buries him in a valley there and no one knows his grave. Israel mourns thirty days, and Joshua, full of the spirit of wisdom, leads in his place.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: 1451 BC, in the last month of the 40th year after the Exodus (Deut 1:3; 34:5-8).

events.name: Israel Crosses the Jordan
events.description: On the tenth day of the first month, the priests bearing the ark step into the Jordan in flood and the waters stand up in a heap; the whole nation crosses on dry ground. Twelve stones from the riverbed are set up at Gilgal as a memorial.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: 1451 BC, forty years after the Exodus (Josh 4:19).

events.name: Period of the Judges
events.description: Between Joshua and the monarchy, Israel cycles through apostasy, oppression, and rescue as God raises deliverers such as Deborah, Gideon, and Samson. Archaeology reveals a surge of small highland villages in this era, the material footprint of early Israel taking root in Canaan's hill country.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: from Joshua's death (c. 1426 BC, estimated) to Saul's accession in 1095 BC. The figures in Judges add up to more than this span; Ussher keeps the 480 years of 1 Kgs 6:1 by measuring each period of rest (Judg 3:11, 3:30, 5:31, 8:28) from the previous deliverance and by running the Ammonite oppression alongside Jair and the Philistine forty years alongside Eli and Samson. Main deliverances: Othniel c. 1405, Ehud c. 1325, Deborah c. 1285, Gideon c. 1245, Jephthah 1188 BC. Mainstream scholarship places the judges c. 1200-1050 BC, many of them regional and overlapping.

events.name: Death of Joshua
events.description: Joshua son of Nun dies at 110 and is buried at Timnath-serah in Mount Ephraim. Israel serves the LORD all his days and the days of the elders who outlived him.
events.dateNotes: Year not given in Scripture; c. 1426 BC follows Josephus's 25 years of leadership after Moses (Antiquities 5.117). Ussher leaves it open between c. 1443 and 1413 BC.

events.name: Deborah Defeats Sisera
events.description: Deborah and Barak defeat Canaanite general Sisera.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: c. 1285 BC, after twenty years of oppression by Jabin (Judg 4:3).

events.name: Gideon Defeats Midian
events.description: Gideon defeats the Midianites with 300 men.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: c. 1245 BC, after seven years of Midianite oppression (Judg 6:1).

events.name: Jephthah Defeats the Ammonites
events.description: Recalled from exile by the elders of Gilead, Jephthah argues Israel's title to the land and then defeats the Ammonites, ending eighteen years of oppression. His vow to offer whatever first came out of his house to meet him falls on his only daughter.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: 1188 BC, ending the eighteen-year oppression begun c. 1206 BC (Judg 10:8).

events.name: Death of Samson
events.description: Blinded and set to grind in the prison at Gaza after Delilah's betrayal, Samson is brought out to entertain the Philistines at a feast to Dagon. Praying for strength one last time, he pulls down the pillars of the temple, killing more Philistines at his death than in his life.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: 1117 BC, after Samson had judged Israel twenty years (Judg 15:20; 16:31).

events.name: Ark Captured by Philistines
events.description: The Philistines capture the Ark of the Covenant at the battle of Aphek. Eli dies upon hearing the news.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: 1116 BC (1 Sam 4:1-22). Eli, aged 98, died on hearing the news, having judged Israel forty years (1 Sam 4:15-18).

people.role: born on the day the ark was taken

events.name: Samuel Judges Israel at Mizpah
events.description: After twenty years of the ark at Kirjath-jearim, Samuel calls Israel to put away their idols and gathers them at Mizpah to fast and confess. When the Philistines attack, the LORD thunders against them and Israel routs them; Samuel sets up the stone Ebenezer, "Hitherto hath the LORD helped us."
events.dateNotes: Ussher: 1096 BC, twenty years after the ark came to Kirjath-jearim (1 Sam 7:2) and a year before Saul.

events.name: Saul Anointed King
events.description: When the people demand a king like the nations, God directs Samuel to anoint Saul of Benjamin as Israel's first monarch. Tall, striking, and initially victorious over Ammon and the Philistines, Saul forfeits his dynasty through disobedience, opening the way for David's rise.
events.dateNotes: Ussher: 1095 BC (AM 2909); Saul reigned forty years (Acts 13:21). Mainstream scholarship places his accession c. 1050 BC.

events.name: David Anointed by Samuel
